title: The nineteen flyers World 1-2 never had
summary: Tallying every object list in the game says which missing enemy costs the most: kind 0x42, nineteen records, all of them in World 1-2. Measuring how it flies, what it does on contact, and which tiles draw it took three emulator runs and a rerun of a survey that had already seen it.

title: The bottom eight pixels
summary: World 1-3 has a corridor with eight pixels of headroom that our twelve-pixel Mario could not enter. The cartridge tests eight of his twelve sideways and five of his eleven overhead, and with both measured the test walk finishes a World 2 level for the first time.

title: The lift was going the wrong way
summary: World 1-2's last gap had one moving platform in it and no search could cross it. The platform had been travelling in the wrong direction since the day it was written, because nobody had asked the cartridge which way a lift sets off.

title: Three heights of a jump
summary: World 1-1 had a pillar Mario could not clear, hidden behind a scripted walker with a jump no player could perform. The cartridge turns out to have three jump heights and this project had only ever measured the shortest.

title: The block that gives way
summary: The most-used object in the cartridge, measured at last by putting Mario on it instead of dropping him on it; Mario's skid pose; and a swimming mechanic this project nearly invented for a game that does not have one.

title: The number that never fitted
summary: A support window of 29 pixels matched no lift width the engine had. Reading the sprites off the running game explains it, and measures the enemies, Mario's poses, and the most common object in the cartridge.

title: Mario stops being a black square
summary: The object atlas was already extracted; finding Mario in it, and naming the object kinds against four bosses.

title: The game draws the cartridge
summary: A separate command had been rendering levels from the ROM at 99.60% since Milestone 2 while the game itself drew grey rectangles. Now the game draws the real tiles, the real status bar, and the one background tile the cartridge animates.

title: The cartridge had a table all along
summary: Six of the twelve levels had been pinned by playing to them. Fifty bytes at the start of each ROM bank name all twelve, and the routine that loads a world's graphics names them too, which is what finally made worlds 3 and 4 draw.

title: World 2 decoded perfectly and drew nonsense
summary: The level decoder could only see one ROM bank, so only World 1 existed. Finding the other eleven levels turned up a pointer that hides its own bank, what the pointers before a level are for, and a Mario who could not fall to his death.

title: Thirteen enemies deleted on frame one
summary: Every enemy past the first screen was being deleted before Mario moved. Fixing it needed the rule the cartridge already uses, and turned up a level whose exit was walled in.

title: The half of the list you never see
summary: A brute-force sweep of memory finds what the object list's skip bit is for, Mario measures 11 by 12 instead of 8 by 8, and the jumper runs off a table.

title: Two walkers and a lift
summary: Measuring what the object kinds actually do: a moving platform Mario rides, and two ground walkers that differ only at a ledge.

title: The table the game reads while you walk
summary: Decoding the cartridge's object list, and measuring what one of its enemies actually does.

title: The levels look like the game now
summary: World 1 drawn from the ROM with the cartridge's own tile graphics, scored at 99.60% of playfield pixels against the emulator. The tile data was in a block everyone already knew about, copied to video RAM addresses nobody had checked.

title: All of World 1, out of the cartridge
summary: Three levels located and pinned by playing to each one, and every column of all three matches the running game. Four explanations for one stuck-at-the-spawn symptom, three of them wrong, and the real cause was that Start pauses the game.

title: Flying Mario through his own level
summary: Only 88 of World 1-1's 300 columns had ever been checked against the real game, because that is where a scripted walker died. Replacing the terrain with a non-solid tile and pinning Mario in the air gets the cartridge to its own exit, and all 300 columns now match.

title: Asking the cartridge which tiles are solid
summary: The solidity rule Rian caught being wrong was fitted to 7 of World 1-1's 43 tile ids. Super Mario Land tests collision against the background tilemap in video RAM, which can be written to, so the game itself classified all 256 ids. Carries a correction: the one tile it called decoration is a coin.

title: The cartridge does not say what is solid
summary: The ROM gives World 1-1's 300 columns but nothing about which tiles stop Mario. Observing that took three attempts, because a 16-pixel-wide Mario laps into every wall he is blocked by and landing clips him into every platform he lands on. Carries a correction: the solidity it concluded was still wrong, and playing the result on the cartridge is what showed it.

title: World 1-1 in fifteen pointers
summary: The column format was only half of it. A level is a list of 16-bit pointers, one per 20-column screen, and World 1-1 reuses three of its fifteen. That explains the repeat the last post treated as a trap, and all 300 columns now decode from the ROM matching the running game on every one.

title: The level was in the cartridge all along
summary: Rian asked why I was driving Mario through World 1-1 to discover its layout when the data should be in the ROM. It is: a run-length column format, decoded here. Getting the starting offset right took two attempts, because the level repeats every 40 columns and a 20-column agreement fits in two places.

title: The status bar was the answer
summary: The star and the Fly are now dropped from the default game, since Super Mario Land has neither. And the search for the score in work RAM turned up 96 changed bytes, while the number was on screen the whole time in tiles that are literally the digits.

title: The numbers were never real
summary: Several sessions of refining an estimate of Mario's world position, each fixing a real bug in the last, and none of them ever checked against anything. Measuring the scroll off the rendered frames shows the walker was jammed against a pipe 3% of the way into the level the whole time.

title: Landing a stomp on purpose
summary: The last unmeasured physics constant. Two attempts failed because they asked the sprite table whether a stomp had happened; the third asked the game's own phase byte, landed 61 real stomps from one save state, and found that a bounce decays like a released jump even with the button held.

title: A promise the code did not keep
summary: An earlier post showed a tuning file changing gravity and jump height. It worked as a function; it was never actually reachable from the game, and would have silently reset on every level change even if it had been. Found and fixed.

title: Shipping the real jump
summary: Measuring the cartridge's three-regime jump and simulating it in the engine turned out to be different jobs. Running the first attempt caught a wrong branch and a fall acceleration that undershot once actually tested end to end.

title: Gravity is not one number
summary: Three sessions of trying to fit a jump to one accelerating curve failed for a reason: it isn't one. Splitting the trace at the apex, and the game's own phase byte confirming the split, reveals three distinct speed regimes instead.

title: The pyramid was never solid
summary: World 1-1's opening pyramid looked like a solid staircase and was assumed to be one. Building it as an actual level and walking it proved otherwise: marked solid, Mario gets stuck at spawn; marked non-solid, he matches every real recording exactly.

title: Jumping instead of waiting
summary: Pausing for an enemy only delays it; jumping at it survives past tile 1880. That exposed a real bug in how far the tilemap tracker could be trusted, fixed by reading Mario's own speed register instead of watching for change.

title: World 1-1 was never stuck
summary: A frozen screen position, a scroll register stuck at zero, and an unavoidable enemy. All three looked like bugs. Watching the emulator instead of trusting single reads resolved every one of them.

title: Giving the sound events a voice
summary: Game emits SoundEvents; the windowed frontend used to throw them away. Wiring an actual audio backend behind the gui feature, and why keeping sound as data made it a small change.

title: Pinning a ROM offset from emulator memory
summary: Extracting the title screen straight from the ROM file broke in a way that looked fine: real tiles, wrong bank. How comparing against the emulator caught it, and the small tool that finds a ROM offset from emulator memory instead of assembly addresses.

title: Power-ups and polish
summary: The flower and its bouncing superball, a star that turns mistakes cheap, a one-way camera, a pause button, and an event-based sound model. Plus a short campaign to play it all in.

title: The physics of walking
summary: Acceleration, friction, and a top speed give the walk its feel, subpixels make slow movement believable, and gravity is the same idea pointed down. All deterministic, all tested headlessly.

title: Build your own level
summary: Levels are plain text and the movement is a handful of tunable numbers, both editable without touching Rust. If you can type, you can make a level.

title: Closing the loop
summary: A finish line, lives that run out, and a state machine tying title to play to win or game over and back. The parts finally become a game you can start, lose, and restart.

title: Blocks, coins, and getting big
summary: Question blocks that answer a headbutt, coins that add up to a life, and a mushroom that turns a fatal hit into a shrink. The pieces that make a level worth exploring.

title: Enemies, stomps, and dying
summary: An enemy that patrols and turns at ledges, a stomp that hinges on who was moving down, and death with a respawn. All tested without ever opening a window.

title: Booting to the title screen
summary: How the first real frame got drawn: verify the ROM, read the title from a headless emulator's video memory, decode the tiles, and render them ourselves. Measured 99.82% match against the emulator.

title: The workspace and how it is driven
summary: What the repo is, the one-task-at-a-time loop that drives it, and the four-module shape of the code.
